summary: Justin Lovell, CEO of The Splash Lab, argues that single-user, unisex-by-default restrooms already solve the gendered public restroom debate. The article draws on Matt Nardella of Moss, Mia Blanchett of HGA, Mary Coakley Munk and Paco Underhill to weigh the benefits and costs of single-user designs, then describes unisex, family and universal restroom layouts and Lovair products that support them.
one_line: Justin Lovell argues single-user, unisex restrooms with smart design already solve the gendered public restroom debate, weighing costs and trade-offs.
key_facts: Justin Lovell is Chief Executive Officer at The Splash Lab and published the article on June 23, 2017.
The article argues that the single-user, unisex-by-default public restroom already solves the gendered restroom controversy.
Matt Nardella, founder of Moss architecture and design studio in Chicago, wrote that 'Clever design solutions can completely resolve the problem posed by gender-specific public restrooms.'
Nardella suggests replacing multi-user partitioned bathrooms with multiple gender-neutral, single-occupancy restrooms, some ADA-compliant and others standard 3x5 stalls.
The 2018 edition of the International Building Code will count single-user restrooms toward the total number of required plumbing fixtures.
According to Mia Blanchett of HGA Architects and Engineers, a 40-square-foot single-user restroom costs about $12,500 to build, versus about $4,300 for a single stall in a multiple-user bathroom.
Mary Coakley Munk, president of the American Restroom Association, said that 'With single-user stalls you can lose the corridors and the large wasted space in front of the stalls.'
Paco Underhill, an environmental psychologist and author of Why We Buy: The Science of Shopping, estimated labor costs for cleaning could be as much as 30 percent higher for single-user restrooms.
Des Moines, Iowa-based supermarket chain CEO Randy Edeker instituted single-user restrooms after seeing one in a Miami hotel five years earlier.
Every large-format store the supermarket chain has built since 2012 contains at least nine individual restrooms for men, women, and the disabled.
Family restrooms may have multiple unisex toilet rooms along with common space for handwashing and diaper changing.
The article says the best universal design falls between unisex and family facilities, offering multiple toilet rooms in a stall-sized footprint with communal handwashing stations.
Lovair solid-surface materials can combine a low, ADA-compliant sink with a higher sink, eliminating separate fixtures.
Hand dryers with adjustable noise levels offer a more comfortable environment for small children, autistic users, and those with sensitive ears.
